background: In November 2026, Europol and international law enforcement partners dismantled infrastructure supporting several malware operations . Among them was CastleRAT, a remote access trojan (RAT) that enabled criminals to remotely control infected computers. Europol provided HIBP with 180k email addresses associated with CastleRAT infections, along with 893k unique passwords observed more than 3M times across accounts used on infected computers. The passwords are now searchable via Pwned Passwords .
how: In November 2026, Europol and international law enforcement partners dismantled infrastructure supporting several malware operations .
outcome: 179,745 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Passwords.
editorial: This entry is not a company that lost its customers' data. It is the other side of the transaction: a remote access trojan, taken down by Europol and its partners, whose infrastructure held what it had collected from infected computers. If your address is in here, the likely story is not that a website you trusted was breached.

It is that a machine you used, or one an account of yours was signed into, was under someone else's control. That changes the advice. Changing one password is the response to a site breach. A RAT sees everything typed on the infected machine, so every password used there should be treated as known, including ones for sites that were never breached at all.

The 893,000 unique passwords Europol shared are now in Pwned Passwords, which is the quickest way to check whether yours is among them. The order matters. Clean or replace the infected device first, then change passwords from a different, trusted device, starting with email, because email resets everything else. Changing passwords on a machine that is still compromised just hands over the new ones.

background: In May 2013, the Russian-language hacking forum YouHack suffered a data breach that was later redistributed as part of a larger corpus of data . The breach exposed 107k forum members' email addresses, usernames, IP addresses and MD5 password hashes, most of which were unsalted. Forum posts also contained email address and password pairs belonging to other victims, bringing the total to 7.2M unique email addresses.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 7,160,849 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, IP addresses, Passwords, Usernames.
editorial: A hacking forum getting hacked is a familiar story, but the numbers here are the interesting part. YouHack had about 107,000 members. This entry lists 7.2 million email addresses. The difference is the forum's own content: members posted email and password pairs taken from other victims, so most people in this set were never members. They were the material being traded. That makes it two breaches in one.

For the members, the exposure is their email, username, IP address and an MD5 password hash, mostly unsalted, which modern hardware reverses quickly for anything but a long random password. For everyone else, it means a password of theirs was already circulating among people who collect them by 2013. Old does not mean harmless.

Password reuse is a habit, and a password from 2013 is often a close variant of one still in use today. If your address is here, check whether you still use that password, or a pattern built from it, anywhere. Our password leak check guide explains how to test it without sending the password itself.

background: In March 2023, data allegedly taken from СберСпасибо (SberSpasibo), the loyalty program of Russian bank Сбербанк (Sberbank), was published online . The data contained records relating to 48M users, including 3.3M unique email addresses alongside phone numbers and dates of birth. Data also included bank card numbers stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes, plus loyalty program details such as membership dates and the redemption of bonus points for partner offers.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 3,288,711 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Bank card numbers, Dates of birth, Email addresses, Loyalty program details, Phone numbers.
editorial: The detail worth understanding here is how the card numbers were stored: as unsalted SHA-1 hashes. That sounds protective, and for passwords it would at least slow an attacker down. For card numbers it does very little. A card number is a short string with a known structure: the first six digits identify the issuer, the last digit is a checksum, and only the digits in between vary.

That is a small enough space to hash every possibility and match the results, so a hashed card number should be treated as an exposed one. The rest of the record is a loyalty program's view of a person: phone number, date of birth, email, membership dates and which partner offers they redeemed bonus points on.

Loyalty data looks trivial but it is behavioural, and it is the kind of detail that makes a fake bank call sound real ("we noticed an unusual redemption on your Spasibo account"). The data was published in March 2023 and reached Have I Been Pwned in November 2026, so it has had years to be used.
If you are a Sberbank customer in this set, the card you held then should be reissued if it has not been already.

background: In November 2025, Harvard University suffered a data breach later linked to a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion attempt . The data contained 851k unique email addresses relating to the university's alumni and fundraising systems, along with extensive profile information for donors, alumni, parents and some faculty, staff and students.

In Harvard's disclosure notice , the university stated that the breach impacted "personal information such as email addresses, telephone numbers, home and business addresses, event attendance, details of donations to the University, and other biographical information pertaining to University fundraising and alumni engagement activities".
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In November 2025, Harvard University suffered a data breach later linked to a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion attempt .
outcome: 850,537 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.

The reported exposed data includes Charitable donations, Citizenship statuses, Dates of birth, Education levels, Email addresses, Employers, Ethnicities, Family members' names, Genders, Job titles, Marital statuses, Names, Occupations, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Places of birth, Salutations, Social media profiles.
editorial: Eighteen data classes is a lot, and the list reads like the fields of a fundraising database, because that is what it came from: alumni engagement and donor records. Charitable donations, family members' names, ethnicities, places of birth, citizenship statuses and marital statuses are not things a university needs to teach anyone. They are things a development office collects to decide whom to ask for money, and how much.

That is the uncomfortable point about this breach. The most detailed profiles belong to the people with the closest relationship to the institution: donors, alumni and parents. Donation history in particular is a ready-made target list, because it says who gives, how much and to what, which is exactly what a fake charity appeal or a fake "alumni office" call needs.

Harvard's notice describes the data as relating to fundraising and alumni engagement. If you are a Harvard alum or donor, expect approaches that cite real gifts, real classmates or real family members. A genuine development office will never object to you hanging up and calling the number on the university's own website.

background: In September 2026, the German political party Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) suffered a data breach which exposed 345k unique email addresses. The following month, hundreds of gigabytes of data containing hundreds of thousands of emails and attachments was published online, with searchable AI-generated summaries and downloadable original files.

An analysis of the incident reported that the breach was detected as early as 9 September, with a subsequent intrusion occurring five days later. In its public statement , AfD attributed the breach to an attack on a hosting provider, identified in subsequent reporting as the party-owned Alternita Dienstleistungs GmbH.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 345,439 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Email messages.
editorial: Two data classes, but one of them is "email messages", and that is the part that matters. An email address list tells you who was on a mailing list. Hundreds of gigabytes of messages and attachments tell you what people wrote to a political party, which under European data protection law counts as special category data because it can reveal political opinions. Have I Been Pwned flags this entry as sensitive.

The publication format is new and worth watching. The data was released with searchable, AI-generated summaries alongside the original files. That lowers the effort needed to find a named person in a leak from days of reading to a single search, which makes the exposure for anyone who merely wrote in, including people who are not members, far greater than the headline count of addresses suggests.

The party attributed the breach to an attack on its hosting provider. Whatever one thinks of the organisation, the lesson is general: correspondence sent to any campaign, charity or advocacy group sits on someone else's servers indefinitely. If you are in this set, assume messages you sent could be quoted back to you, and treat any contact that references them with caution.

background: In September 2024, the French national pension fund Assurance Retraite suffered a data breach affecting approximately 370k assistance beneficiaries . The data included 70k unique email addresses along with names, dates of birth, physical addresses, phone numbers, income levels, marital statuses, French social security numbers (NIR) and contact details of relatives or other nominated contacts. In its disclosure notice, Assurance Retraite attributed the breach to a compromised partner account .
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 70,372 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Family members' names, Government issued IDs, Income levels, Marital statuses, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: The people in this set were assistance beneficiaries of France's national pension fund, and the record makes their circumstances plain: income levels and marital statuses sit alongside names, addresses, phone numbers and French social security numbers (NIR). It is hard to design a better list for fraud aimed at vulnerable people. The field that stands out is the contact details of relatives or other nominated contacts.

That turns one person's record into a small family tree, and it enables the scam where a caller claims to be from the pension fund, already knows the beneficiary's details, and asks a son or daughter to help "update the file" or pay a fee to keep the benefit. The cause, a compromised partner account, is also typical.

Large public bodies increasingly share data with service partners, and the partner is often the weaker link. If you or a relative receive support from l'Assurance retraite, treat any call asking for bank details or a fee as fraud. Hang up and call back on the number from an official letter you already have.

breaches.name: GitesDeFrance
breaches.title: Gîtes de France
breaches.summary: In May 2026, the French holiday rental network Gîtes de France suffered a data breach affecting some of its departmental branches. The incident exposed hundreds of thousands of customer records, including 118k unique email addresses alongside names, phone numbers, postal addresses and booking details.

background: In May 2026, the French holiday rental network Gîtes de France suffered a data breach affecting some of its departmental branches. The incident exposed hundreds of thousands of customer records, including 118k unique email addresses alongside names, phone numbers, postal addresses and booking details.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 117,574 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Booking details, Email addresses, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: Gîtes de France operates through departmental branches, and the breach affected some of them rather than the whole network. A branch structure is common for federations, franchises and cooperatives, and it tends to mean many separate systems with uneven security, any one of which can expose customers who only ever dealt with the national brand. The data class that sets this apart is booking details.

A holiday booking says where someone will be and, by implication, when their home will be empty. Combined with a postal address, that is information a burglar would value, though for most people the more likely misuse is fraud: a message about "your upcoming stay" that knows the property, the dates and the guest's name, asking for a deposit to be paid again or a card to be re-confirmed.

Holiday rental scams already rely on urgency and plausibility. A leak that supplies the real booking removes the main thing that used to give them away. If you booked through a Gîtes de France branch, confirm any payment request directly with the owner or branch using contact details from your original confirmation, never from the message asking for money.

background: In January 2026, the private company intelligence platform Crunchbase was targeted in a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion attempt . Data allegedly obtained from the company was subsequently published publicly and included 560k unique email addresses, largely belonging to leads and business contacts. Other data included names, physical addresses, phone numbers, job titles, employers and LinkedIn profiles. Crunchbase later confirmed that a threat actor had exfiltrated documents from its corporate network.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In January 2026, the private company intelligence platform Crunchbase was targeted in a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion attempt .
outcome: 559,908 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Employers, Job titles, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Social media profiles.
editorial: There is an irony in a company-intelligence platform losing its own contact data. Crunchbase is in the business of organising information about businesses and the people in them, and what leaked was largely its leads and business contacts: names, employers, job titles, phone numbers, addresses and LinkedIn profiles. The LinkedIn field is what makes this set unusually ready to use.

Most leaked contact lists need some work before an attacker can be sure the person and the job are current. A profile link does that work: it confirms the role, shows the reporting line and supplies the photo and history needed to impersonate a colleague or a recruiter convincingly. Crunchbase later confirmed that documents were exfiltrated from its corporate network, so this is not only a scraped list.

Founders, investors and executives are over-represented in a dataset like this, and they are the usual targets for fake investment offers, fake board introductions and invoice fraud. If you are in it, be sceptical of unsolicited deal flow that seems to know exactly who you are and who you work with.

background: In August 2026, the digital health company Sharecare was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion campaign . The group subsequently published data it claimed was taken from Sharecare's systems, containing 318k unique email addresses. Most of the data consisted of B2B sales and marketing records with names, physical addresses, phone numbers, job titles and employers.
The data also included a small number of Brazilian health insurance plan members, including dates of birth, genders, marital statuses and CPF numbers (Brazilian taxpayer identification numbers).
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In August 2026, the digital health company Sharecare was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion campaign .
outcome: 318,185 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Employers, Genders, Government issued IDs, Job titles, Marital statuses, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: Most of this data is B2B sales and marketing records, the same kind of business contact list that appears in several other ShinyHunters releases. Read only the headline and you would file it as a nuisance. The detail that changes that is in the last line of the record: a small number of Brazilian health plan members, with dates of birth, genders, marital statuses and CPF numbers.

A CPF is Brazil's taxpayer identification number, and it is used far more widely than its name suggests: opening bank accounts, signing up for phone contracts, buying online, and proving identity to almost any service. Paired with a name and date of birth it is enough to attempt credit and account fraud in that person's name.

A small number of records can carry more real harm than hundreds of thousands of work email addresses. That is a pattern worth recognising in breach reporting generally. The size of a set and its severity are different measurements. If you hold a Brazilian plan connected to Sharecare, monitoring your CPF for new credit activity matters more here than changing any password.

editorial: This is one of a run of entries in the archive with the same shape: a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" demand, followed by publication of what is mostly corporate contact data. Neogen's set is mailing lists, employee records and business contacts, so most people in it are not customers in the consumer sense. They are buyers, suppliers, lab staff and people who once filled in a form.

Contact records sound harmless until you look at what they combine: name, salutation, employer, job title, direct phone number and work address. That is the exact kit needed for a convincing business email compromise.

An invoice that appears to come from a real supplier, addressed to the right person by title, and followed up by a phone call to their actual desk number is far more persuasive than a generic phishing email. If your work address is in this set, the people to warn are colleagues in accounts payable.
Any request to change a supplier's bank details, especially one that arrives with urgency, should be confirmed by calling a number you already had on file, not one in the message.

fields.name: Physical addresses
fields.why: Where someone actually lives. Combined with a name this moves the risk off the internet.

fields.name: Phone numbers
fields.why: Enables SIM-swap attacks against SMS two-factor codes, and puts the number on scam-call lists indefinitely.

fields.name: Employers
fields.why: Connects a personal account to a workplace, which is how attackers pivot from a person to a company.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: An exposed address may be used in phishing attempts. Treat unexpected messages with caution.

fields.name: Job titles
fields.why: Identifies who has access to what, which is how targets for business email compromise are picked.

fields.name: Salutations
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

actions: Move two-factor authentication off SMS and onto an authenticator app, which a SIM swap cannot intercept.
Be sceptical of post and callers who already know your address, knowing it is no longer evidence of anything.
Be alert to phishing. A message may use details from exposed or collected records to appear familiar; verify requests through the service directly.
